label: react-form-react-hook-form-validation-en
top_ai_sentences:
Controller is the way to go for components that don't expose a plain ref, like React Native's
TextInput:
mode: "onBlur" gives users feedback earlier.
The result is a form that's type-safe and fast, with validation rules in one place.
If you want feedback before the user hits submit, use mode: "onBlur" or mode: "onChange".

For simple cases you can pass rules directly to register, like register("name", { required:
true, minLength: 2 }).

For
repeated or dynamic fields, useFieldArray is much safer than managing array indices manually.

It's also the right call for large forms where
every keystroke shouldn't trigger a re-render, and for integrating with UI libraries such as
shadcn/ui, Material UI, or Chakra.
For a form with one or two fields, a bit of useState and a manual check is enough.

If you need
rich visual feedback on every keystroke, a fully controlled component might be simpler.

When
the form is split across child components, use FormProvider to avoid prop drilling.

Set defaultValues for every field; react-hook-form works better with initial values, especially
for checkboxes and selects.
Without them, checkboxes and selects can end up undefined.

And
obviously, it only works in React.

Add
@hookform/resolvers/zod and the form validates against the schema while the values come out
already
typed.
For number inputs, add valueAsNumber: true so the parsed value is actually a number, not a string.

Number inputs return strings by default, so z.number() rejects
    them unless you add valueAsNumber: true.
Derive the form type from the Zod schema with z.infer<typeof schema> instead of duplicating it.

Keep
validation rules inside the Zod schema rather than scattering them across the component.

For
performance guidance, see [When to Use useMemo and
useCallback](/recipes/react-usememo-usecallback-performance/).

react-hook-form keeps re-renders low by registering uncontrolled inputs instead of tracking every
keystroke.
Zod becomes worth it once the schema grows or you want to reuse it in more than one form.
zod lets you write a validation schema and pull a TypeScript type out of it.

This combo shines when validation gets messy: conditional rules, cross-field checks, async
server-side checks, nested objects, or field arrays.

register returns props for uncontrolled inputs,
    so don't layer your own value and onChange on top.

Always pass the generic so useForm<FormData>({ resolver:
    zodResolver(schema) }) gives you typed values.
